title: The Great Banquet and the Cost of Following

verses.text: One Sabbath, Jesus went to eat in the home of a leading Pharisee, and those in attendance were watching Him closely.
Right there before Him was a man with dropsy.
So Jesus asked the experts in the law and the Pharisees, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?"
But they remained silent. Then Jesus took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way.
And He asked them, "Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?"
And they were unable to answer these questions.
When Jesus noticed how the guests chose the places of honor, He told them a parable:
"When you are invited to a wedding banquet, do not sit in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited.
Then the host who invited both of you will come and tell you, 'Give this man your seat.' And in humiliation, you will have to take the last place.

But when you are invited, go and sit in the last place, so that your host will come and tell you, 'Friend, move up to a better place.' Then you will be honored in front of everyone at the table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted."

Then Jesus said to the man who had invited Him, "When you host a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors. Otherwise, they may invite you in return, and you will be repaid.
But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind,
and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous."
When one of those reclining with Him heard this, he said to Jesus, "Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God."
But Jesus replied, "A certain man prepared a great banquet and invited many guests.
When it was time for the banquet, he sent his servant to tell those who had been invited, 'Come, for everything is now ready.'
But one after another they all began to make excuses. The first one said, 'I have bought a field, and I need to go see it. Please excuse me.'
Another said, 'I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to try them out. Please excuse me.'
Still another said, 'I have married a wife, so I cannot come.'

The servant returned and reported all this to his master. Then the owner of the house became angry and said to his servant, 'Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.'
'Sir,' the servant replied, 'what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.'
So the master told his servant, 'Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, so that my house will be full.
For I tell you, not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.'"
Now large crowds were traveling with Jesus, and He turned and said to them,
If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life— he cannot be My disciple.
And whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple.
Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?
Otherwise, if he lays the foundation and is unable to finish the work, everyone who sees it will ridicule him,
saying, 'This man could not finish what he started to build.'
Or what king on his way to war with another king will not first sit down and consider whether he can engage with ten thousand men the one coming against him with twenty thousand?
And if he is unable, he will send a delegation while the other king is still far off, to ask for terms of peace.
In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple.
Salt is good, but if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned?
It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear."

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Table-talk and teaching: a Sabbath healing and three meal-time lessons, followed by street-side sayings about discipleship
context.audience: A leading Pharisee's dinner guests, including experts in the law, and then the large crowds traveling with Jesus. Luke's wider readers learn that the banquet of God is open to the poor and outsiders.
context.mapLabel: A PHARISEE'S HOUSE, ON THE ROAD TO JERUSALEM
context.setting: Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem (13:22) and spends a Sabbath meal in the home of a leading Pharisee. The Sabbath dinner was a main social event of the week, and those invited were chosen carefully. The guests are "watching Him closely" (v.1), so what looks like a friendly meal is partly a trap. The chapter ends outdoors, where large crowds are traveling with Him (v.25).
context.custom: Seating at a banquet followed rank: the places nearest the host were the places of honor, and guests jockeyed for them (v.7). Invitations were an exchange, since a dinner was expected to be repaid with another dinner (v.12). In the great banquet parable, a host sent a first invitation well ahead and a second on the day itself ("Come, for everything is now ready," v.17), so guests who had already said yes and then backed out were insulting him.
context.timelineImmediate: Luke 13 closed with Jesus' lament over Jerusalem and the warning that the door will not stay open. Chapter 14 moves inside to a table where those who think they are first face Him, and then back out to the road to make clear what it costs to follow. Luke 15 will show the lost being welcomed, so this chapter sets the cost and the invitation side by side.
context.timelineBible: The banquet is a common biblical image of the final day, as in Isaiah 25:6-8 where God prepares a feast for all peoples. The man who says "Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God" (v.15) speaks the common hope. Jesus' parable replies that the invited have already been called and are not coming, so the feast goes to the poor and the outsider.
context.sparkNotes: At a Sabbath dinner Jesus heals a man with dropsy, silences the experts with a question about a rescued ox, and tells guests who are fighting for the best seats to take the lowest place. He tells the host to invite those who cannot repay him, and then tells a parable about a banquet whose invited guests all make excuses, so the host fills his hall from the streets and roads. Outside, to large crowds, He sets the price of discipleship: loving Him above everything, carrying a cross, and counting the cost like a builder and a king, since salt that has lost its taste is good for nothing.

translation.meaning: A medical word meaning a man swollen with fluid, from hydōr, "water." Luke is the only Gospel writer to use it, and the term fits a physician. Dropsy was a cruel disease in which the body swells and the thirst never ends.

In Hebrew and Aramaic speech, "hate" often meant "love less" or "choose second." Jesus is using a sharp comparison, not asking for hatred of family. Matthew 10:37 says the same thing as "loves more than Me." The point is that no loyalty may stand above Him.
To urge strongly or press, here in the sense of insistent invitation to people who feel unworthy to come in. The host does not force anyone but wants his house full.
Literally to calculate the expense with pebbles, as people did before written arithmetic. Jesus asks would-be followers to do the sum before they commit.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's parable of the wedding feast, which has similarities with this parable but differs in setting and details.
Matthew's Sabbath argument from a sheep fallen into a pit.
Loving family more than Jesus, and taking up the cross.
Salt that loses its saltiness, in the Sermon on the Mount.
Mark's saying about salt that loses its flavor.

otBackground.note: "Do not claim a place among his great men; it is better for him to say to you, 'Come up here.'" The proverb behind Jesus' advice on seats.
The Lord of hosts prepares a banquet for all peoples, the picture behind the man's cry about eating at the feast of God.
God's people were to care for the poor and the stranger, the kind of guests Jesus tells the host to invite.
Honor your father and mother. The call to put Christ first in verse 26 sets this command in its place and does not cancel it.

commentary.note: Henry sees the invited guests who refuse as the Jews who had every offer and turned it down, and the poor gathered from the streets as the Gentiles and the outcasts. His warning is plain: "They that will not have Christ when they may shall not have him when they would." On the host who should invite the poor, he says charity is not a loss, since those who give to the helpless "shall in no wise lose their reward." On the seats, he says: "The way to rise high is to begin low."

On the cost of discipleship, Henry says that Christ wants no one to follow Him blindly, so He lays out the price before anyone starts. The builder and the king show that a half-finished tower or a lost war is worse than never beginning. Henry also stresses that grace is sufficient to finish what is begun. On the salt, he says that a Christian who has lost his savor is "the most useless worthless thing in the world."

Gill describes dropsy as a "preternatural collection of serum, or water in some part of the body," and thinks the Pharisees may have placed the man there to see whether Jesus would heal on the Sabbath. On "hate" in verse 26, he rejects a literal reading: Christ does not command ill will toward family, but disciples must not prefer relatives to Him and must be ready to set aside family opposition for His service. On the tower and the king he calls for counting the cost before taking up the Christian profession, trusting God's strength more than one's own.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 14, but his chapter "The Great Sin" in Mere Christianity bears on verses 7-11. He calls pride the utmost evil and the sin behind all others, and says it is essentially competitive: the proud person takes pleasure in being above others, not simply in having something. That is exactly the dinner scene, where guests are fighting over seats near the host. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: At a Sabbath dinner, Jesus heals a man and tells guests to take the lowest seat and invite those who cannot repay. He tells of a great banquet whose guests make excuses, then tells the crowds to count the cost of following Him.
overview.settingLine: A Pharisee's Sabbath dinner, then the road.

history.t: These meals were a main social event, and the guest list was carefully chosen.
Seating showed rank, so taking the best seat risked public embarrassment.

customs.t: Seats nearest the host were places of honor, and guests competed for them.
A dinner was expected to be repaid, so inviting the poor broke the pattern.

archaeology.t: Wealthy homes in Jerusalem had dining rooms built for reclining guests.
Large stone jars, used for purity and wine, are common finds in Jewish homes.

overview.discussion: Jesus says we must "hate" family to follow Him. What do you think He means?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
